content.title: About
content.content: Cassava flour is made from the dried and ground root of the cassava plant (Manihot esculenta). It is a gluten‑free flour with a neutral taste, commonly used in gluten‑free baking, sauces, and breading.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cassava is a staple food in tropical Africa, South America, and Southeast Asia.
Cassava starch has a high thickening power, making it a popular thickener for soups and sauces.
Cassava flour can replace wheat flour 1:1, but often requires a binder (e.g., xanthan gum) in gluten‑free recipes.
Raw cassava contains cyanogenic glycosides, so the root is usually washed and cooked at high temperatures to remove toxins.
Cassava flour has a higher glycemic index than most whole grains.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Suitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Provides a quick source of energy, useful for high‑energy needs.

items.title: Rich in potassium
items.content: Potassium helps maintain fluid balance and normal blood pressure.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Fits well into low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Can cause rapid blood sugar spikes; people with diabetes should use it in moderation.

items.title: Cyanogenic compounds
items.content: Improperly processed cassava may contain toxins; use only commercially processed flour.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Rare, but possible allergic reactions to cassava.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cassava flour is used in gluten‑free baking (bread, muffins, pancakes), as a coating, in sauces, puddings, and as a thickener for soups. It can be blended with other gluten‑free flours to improve texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For long‑term storage keep it in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent mold growth.
